Series intro on veteran suicide; two content-plan statements, one with an embedded hedged claim about emerging anti-suicide treatments.
dTMS for OCD remission data (author is coauthor). One borderline efficacy generalization. The ChatGPT-generated prior-auth letter template was not logged (not the author's claim).

Defense of Cerebral against the WSJ/Gimlet podcast. Two causal claims about media reporting and suicide risk logged as borderline. Counterfactuals about the past case and quoted AACAP guidance not logged.
Satirical fictional HR dialogue with Santa; no sincere forward-looking claims about the world.
Satirical Christmas poem about Elon Musk; events described are past (Tesla share sales, Twitter layoffs); no sincere forward-looking claims.
Promo for Let's Rethink This and First Tracks (author's employer). One conditional hopeful claim that appears to be an excerpt from Jerry Ashton's article.

statements.quote: Maybe I’ll handle the other points in a subsequent article.
statements.context: Opening of the open letter on Mayor Eric Adams' 11-point plan. The author addresses only point one (police bringing people in for involuntary psychiatric care on a looser standard) and may cover the other points in a later article.
statements.note: Own content plan; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: By reducing the standard of risk by which someone can be brought in the door, you limit information which determines who is a risk or not.
statements.context: Addressed to Mayor Adams. Consequence claim about the NYC directive that lets police bring people to psychiatric ERs on a risk standard below imminent danger: ER doctors will have less information to judge who is a risk.
statements.note: Consequence claim about a directive not yet in effect; present tense.

statements.quote: By changing the standard by which people can be brought in, you hamper our ability to do a good job of caring for those same humans.
statements.context: Same argument: the directive will degrade ER psychiatrists' ability to gather collateral information and care for the people brought in.
statements.note: Consequence claim; present tense.

statements.quote: Because we won’t know why they’re presenting for care. And if we don’t have EMS there, I strongly doubt we’re going to get a great medical history.
statements.context: Predicted effect of the directive on ER evaluations: without police or EMS context on dangerousness, doctors will not know why the person was brought in and will not get a good medical history. Author cites Eric Garner's death as an example of a missed medical condition.
statements.note: Conditional ('if we don't have EMS there').

statements.quote: Your executive order makes our job much more difficult. Crucially, even if your officers are told to ignore mental hygiene law, we can’t. If someone is brought in for evaluation because your officers found them in a park, we still can’t legally admit them, as physicians, because we would lose our licenses by admitting patients in contravention of mental health law around involuntary commitment.
statements.context: Prediction that under the Adams directive, people brought in by police on the lower standard will not be admissible by physicians under New York mental hygiene law, so the order will make ER work harder without producing admissions.
statements.note: Compound: effect on ER work plus a legal-conditional claim. Restated in footnote 2 (separate entry).

statements.quote: Involuntary care creates mistrust. It’s terrifying. It’s rarely helpful. At best, it’s going to lead to a lot of overworked emergency doctors. It will also lead to patients with even less trust in the police and healthcare than they already have.
statements.context: Section 'This Is a Bad Idea'. Predicted outcomes of the Adams involuntary-removal directive: more overworked emergency doctors and less patient trust in police and healthcare.
statements.confidence_phrase: it’s going to lead to / It will also lead to
statements.note: Compound: two predicted consequences plus general claims about involuntary care.

statements.quote: If you want to help homeless humans who are suffering, actually propose something that’s intended to help them. They will say YES if it’s understood as helpful!
statements.context: Conditional prediction: if the city proposes services that are genuinely helpful, homeless people with mental illness will accept them voluntarily.
statements.note: Conditional; first sentence is advice, second is predictive.

statements.quote: Dear Eric Adams, and all policy makers: create helpful solutions! People will want those, voluntarily, without coercion.
statements.context: Closing appeal of the open letter; prediction that people will voluntarily take up helpful, non-coercive solutions.
statements.note: Restates the previous conditional; imperative plus prediction.

statements.quote: Frankly, I’m close to certain the Mayor’s order violates mental hygiene law in NYS.
statements.context: Footnote 2. Legal opinion that the Adams order (police transport on a standard below the §9.39 emergency admission standard) violates New York State mental hygiene law.
entities: New York State mental hygiene law
statements.note: Present-state legal opinion, not a forecast; logged for the explicit confidence phrase. A later court ruling could bear on it.

statements.quote: It would mean that the people being brought by NYPD to the psych ER would be evaluated by doctors who would then be legally … UNABLE TO ADMIT THEM TO THE HOSPITAL ANYWAY
statements.context: Footnote 2 conclusion: under the directive, people transported by NYPD on the lower standard would be evaluated and then found legally inadmissible under the §9.39 and §9.27 admission standards.
statements.note: Conditional consequence claim; restates the main-text claim. The ellipsis is the author's own.

statements.quote: I am hereby willing to provide forensic testimony as an expert witness against Eric Adams and the City of New York should they chose to enforce this decree.
statements.context: Footnote 3, addressed to the ACLU and Mental Health Legal Council: conditional pledge to testify as an expert witness if the city enforces the directive.
statements.note: Own conditional commitment, not a world-state forecast. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: So, I’m going to be writing about those treatments that we already have evidence for in cases such as this. Treatments that work for people who are struggling with suicidal thoughts. I am also going to be writing about emerging options that could reduce the risk of completed suicide for people struggling with thinking about it. I’ll discuss how these options apply in veteran populations.
statements.context: Series intro on ending veteran suicide (44 veteran suicides per day; no oral antidepressant tested in suicidal people). The author plans articles on evidence-based treatments for suicidal people and on emerging options; embedded hedged claim that emerging options could reduce completed suicide.
statements.confidence_phrase: I’m going to be writing / could reduce
statements.note: Compound: content plan plus hedged clinical claim about emerging anti-suicide treatments. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I’m going to be writing about the fact that hope exists, even for those who are really struggling.
statements.context: Same series intro; content plan for the veteran suicide series.
statements.note: Own content plan; low forecast value.

statements.quote: Unlike the treatments that got people a little bit better, for a third of people treated with dTMS, they can have remission of symptoms from OCD.
statements.context: Post on BrainsWay H7 coil deep TMS for OCD. Real-world data in Brain Stimulation (author is a coauthor): 46 of 145 patients remitted on Y-BOCS (31.7%). The author generalizes that about a third of people treated with dTMS can reach remission and says clinicians can now treat OCD with real hope.
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense generalization of published real-world data to future patients. Author is a coauthor of the cited study.

statements.quote: In their attempt to create sensational journalism, they document a standard of care, and create a standard of hopelessness, which increases the risk for listeners and non-listeners alike.
statements.context: Defense of Cerebral against episode 3 of the WSJ/Gimlet podcast 'Uncontrolled Substances' about a 17-year-old patient's suicide. Claim that the WSJ reporting increases suicide risk for the public.
statements.note: Borderline causal-effect claim (media coverage raises suicide risk); present tense, ongoing effect.

statements.quote: The very short summary is that reporting graphically about means by which one can kill themselves, which is what the Wall Street Journal was doing, is a way to get more completed suicide, not less.
statements.context: Footnote 3, citing the author's earlier writing on responsible suicide reporting: the WSJ's graphic description of lethal means will produce more completed suicides.
statements.confidence_phrase: is a way to get more
statements.note: Borderline: general causal claim applied to a specific outlet; effect claim about future suicides.

statements.quote: Can we ever hope for a time when those numbers abate, and the tragedies recede? Yes, if we just take lessons from the much-beloved movie classic, It’s a Wonderful Life and bring them into practice in our own lives.
statements.context: Promo for Jerry Ashton (Let's Rethink This, RIP Medical Debt) and First Tracks, a public benefit corporation where the author works. The passage under 'It's a Wonderful Life and Veteran Suicide' appears to be an excerpt from Ashton's article: veteran suicides (44 per day) can abate if people apply the movie's lessons.
statements.note: Appears to be third-party text reproduced approvingly ('Read more in Jerry's new article'). Vague conditional hope, not a testable call.

statements.quote: I think it’s possible to create psychiatric hospitalization that would work more like medical hospitalizations, with procedural care, rapid acting interventions, and complex treatments that require the kind of nursing care that hospitals provide.
statements.context: Essay arguing the data show psychiatric hospitalization does not reduce suicide (Denmark, US veteran, meta-analysis, Brazil data). The author says he would be thrilled to be proven wrong and thinks a procedural, rapid-intervention inpatient model is possible; notes only 1 in 10 US hospitals has ECT access.
statements.note: Possibility claim; no horizon.

statements.quote: We now have a whole array of treatments that have either gotten FDA approval, or are very close. These treatments work rapidly, and they work in ways that are dramatically better than traditional psychiatric treatment.
statements.context: Section 'The Future Could Actually Be Bright'. Claim that rapid-acting treatments are FDA approved or near approval. The next paragraph names SAINT and HOPE TMS (remission in five days), Rotational Field TMS, MDMA, psilocybin and ECT.
statements.note: Implicit regulatory forecast: unnamed treatments 'very close' to FDA approval. Compound with an efficacy claim.

statements.quote: depression can be in remission in five days. That takes brain scanners, equipment, technicians, staffing, and is therefor well suited to inpatient settings.
statements.context: Same section: with fMRI-guided accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (SAINT and HOPE TMS), depression can be in remission in five days; because it needs scanners and staff, the author says it is well suited to inpatient settings, implying a future inpatient role.
entities: fMRI-guided accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense efficacy and fit claim implying future inpatient adoption of SAINT-style TMS.

statements.quote: Rotational Field TMS is on the horizon.
statements.context: Same section, listing rapid-acting treatments coming to inpatient psychiatry after SAINT and HOPE TMS.
statements.note: Flat near-term availability claim for a TMS technology; no date. Area could also be company_market.

statements.quote: MDMA and psilocybin take hours of therapist time in controlled settings, which is actually pretty well suited to inpatient stays.
statements.context: Same section. MDMA- and psilocybin-assisted therapy are presented as future inpatient treatments; the text groups them with treatments that have FDA approval 'or are very close'.
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense fit claim that presupposes MDMA and psilocybin therapy becoming available inpatient treatments.

statements.quote: Inpatient psychiatric hospitalization could be the place where things are done that can’t be done otherwise. That would produce dramatically better outcomes. The hospital could be something other than a place for patients to become even more more at risk. In the future, psychiatric hospitalization can be much better.
statements.context: Closing of 'The Future Could Actually Be Bright': hedged forecast that inpatient psychiatry rebuilt around rapid procedural treatments (accelerated TMS, psychedelics, ECT) can produce much better outcomes.
statements.note: Hedged, undated vision statement; compound with 'would produce dramatically better outcomes'.

statements.quote: I will take this moment to continue my ongoing campaign to remind the Nobel committee that Dr. Nolan Williams should be the recipient of the 2024 Nobel prize in medicine for his groundbreaking work on Stanford accelerated intelligent neuromodulation treatment.
statements.context: Footnote 2 on SAINT: the author's running 'campaign' that Nolan Williams should win the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for Stanford accelerated intelligent neuromodulation treatment.
statements.note: Advocacy ('should'), not a prediction; half-joking 'ongoing campaign'. Logged for the dated, resolvable target.

statements.quote: In the next installment of this, we will review in common language magnetic resonance imaging. I’m not gonna drown you in math either. This will also include information about functional magnetic resonance imaging!
statements.context: 'Coming up next!' section of a medical-imaging explainer series (this part covers x-ray, CT, fluoroscopy and angiogram). Plan for the next installment: MRI and fMRI.
statements.note: Own content plan; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: After that, we will get two more esoteric scans like PET, FDG-PET, and even SPECT
statements.context: Same section: a later installment on PET, FDG-PET and SPECT, with a promised look at the evidence around SPECT (the modality the author associates with Daniel Amen).
